Writing Domain Overview

The Writing domain provides the tools for both structured narrative (like game design) and fluid discovery-based writing (like novel drafting). It is built on a "Graph, Not Tree" philosophy to support non-linear thinking.

🧬 Core Concept: Graph-Based Storytelling

Unlike traditional hierarchical systems that force a rigid parent-child structure, the GaDeMa writing engine treats all narrative elements as nodes in a flexible graph. This allows writers to move between high-level planning and granular drafting without being constrained by structural rules.

The Hierarchy of Intent

Level Entity Role
Container Story The overarching work (e.g., a novel, campaign, or game).
Segment Chapter An organizational unit used to group scenes and manage pacing.
Unit of Work Scene The primary canvas for writing; the intersection of narrative intent and character state.

Note on Non-Linear Elements: Elements like StoryOutlines (the macro structure) and StoryBeats (narrative milestones) exist alongside this hierarchy. They are not locked into a rigid tree; instead, they act as landmarks that can be linked to Chapters or Scenes, allowing your narrative structure to evolve organically.

🧠 Design Philosophy: Structure as a Choice

The system is designed to accommodate two distinct creative modes:

1. The Structural Approach (Planning-First)

Used by designers who think in pacing and architecture. They define the Story and Chapters first, establishing the structural milestones (Beats) before populating them with detailed Scenes. Example: A Game Designer planning "Act I" \(\rightarrow\) "Chapter 1" \(\rightarrow\) "Tutorial Encounter".

2. The Discovery Approach (Writing-First)

Used by authors who write non-linearly. They create Scenes as they come to them, without a predefined structure. Later, they use Chapters and Outlines to group these scenes into a coherent narrative arc. Example: A Novelist writing "The Discovery Scene" and "The Climax" separately, then organizing them into chapters later.

🛠️ Key Features for Narrative Control

  • Flexible Outlining: Outlines are not rigid templates; they are annotations that can be attached to any level (Story, Chapter, or Scene) to provide scaffolding without being mandatory.
  • Bi-directional Linking: Because the system is a graph, you can link elements across different levels (e.g., a Beat referencing a specific Scene) without breaking the hierarchy.
  • View Mode Separation:
    • PrivateWriting: For the messy, iterative drafting process.
    • Presentation: For viewing the polished, structural narrative for review or export.

⚙️ Technical implementation

Concept Implementation Detail
Structural Integrity Uses a graph structure where relationships are explicit links rather than rigid inheritance.
Collapsible Hierarchy Supports hierarchical view (Story \(\rightarrow\) Chapter \(\rightarrow\) Scene) for high-level overview without losing detail.
The Nexus (Scene) The Scene acts as the intersection between static narrative structure and dynamic character state.
